Philippine bonds are the most vulnerable in emerging Asia to a hawkish Federal Reserve, according to an analysis by Bloomberg.
The nation’s sovereign debt was the worst performer in the region during the two most recent episodes of Fed tightening, namely those that began in 2017 and 2022. Philippine 10-year yields climbed by an average of 152 basis points during those periods — nearly four times as much as those of second-placed India.

Technology shares sold off for a second consecutive day as another round of disappointing earnings accelerated a rotation out of the artificial intelligence trade and drove investors toward haven assets such as Treasuries. Crude oil gained.
Futures for the Nasdaq 100 Index slid 2% after earnings from Amazon.com Inc. and Intel Corp. raised fresh concerns about capital expenditure. Amazon slumped 7.3% in extended trading, while Intel plunged 23%. Bitcoin fell 0.5% to about $78,400 after Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, suspended all deposits and withdrawals as it investigated a suspected hack.

Long-dated government bonds spent much of the year punishing anyone brave enough to own them. Now yields are high enough that investors are coming back.
Risk-free payouts near multi-decade highs are becoming difficult to resist, particularly with stocks looking expensive and volatile. Ten-year US Treasuries yields peaked at almost 5.4% this month, their highest since 2002, while those in Japan reached a 30-year high of 3.14%.

By Aya Wagatsuma and Momoka YokoyamaOctober 30, 2026 at 5:48 AM UTCBookmark
Save
Japanese equities shrugged off the Bank of Japan’s surprise move to accelerate selling of its massive holdings of exchange-traded funds, as investors showed confidence in the market’s ability to absorb the extra supply.
Alongside its widely expected decision to keep interest rates unchanged, the BOJ announced Friday it would nearly triple the pace of ETF sales starting in January to about ¥860 billion ($5.5 billion) per year. The Nikkei 225 Stock Average, which was under selling pressure from the morning amid a global tech selloff, pared losses slightly to trade roughly 2% lower in the afternoon.

Takeaways by Bloomberg AI
Oil rose on signs the US may resume military strikes against Iran, risking fresh turbulence in the region that may hurt energy flows.
Brent futures for December, which expire later on Friday, climbed above $116 a barrel, while the more-active January contract was near $112. A top commander briefed President Donald Trump on military options on Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reported. The US leader has repeatedly given signals he may restart airstrikes against Tehran after midterm elections next week.

Takeaways by Bloomberg AI
Asian chip stocks are taking another hit from US tech earnings, with Intel Corp.’s weak outlook raising concerns about semiconductor demand while Amazon.com Inc.’s post-results slump further sours sentiment toward the AI trade.
The declines extend a rough stretch for technology stocks as investors become less forgiving of earnings disappointments after a powerful AI-driven rally. A Bloomberg gauge of Asian chipmakers dropped as much as 4.8% Friday. South Korea’s SK Hynix Inc. and Japan’s Advantest Corp. fell more than 9% each before paring losses, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. dipped over 2%.
